doc.title: Stanley Kay interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Idols and friends: Mandel, Sweets Edison, Snooky Young
summary: Kay compares playing with Buddy to the major leagues, and recalls Johnny Mandel, Sweets Edison and Snooky Young, who was in the Hines Brothers act he managed.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Where I used to sit, yeah. I know where I used to sit. I wanted to look over the band, so I could see what everybody’s doing. And then when we played it, you know, when I got to do it the first time, it was like — I know a lot of baseball players. I’m an entertainment director of the New York Yankees also. And I’ve been with Mr. Steinbrenner for a lot of years. And I ask ball players, I ask like certain guys, I say, “how did you feel when you — your first major league game, you went to the major leagues? How did you feel?” And they would tell me — well I felt the same like they did. Because that’s the major league. When you’re playing with a big name band like Buddy, that’s the major league. And we had great guys in it. I mean I talked to Johnny Mandel the other day. Johnny played bass trumpet in a band, Mandel. And I’d say, “John,” I said, “you’re Johnny Mandel,” I says, “you know how happy I am that you wrote ‘The Shadow of Your Smile’ and ‘Emily’ and did all that on the Army show.” You know which one. Help me someone.

And we talk, and I’m happy for those guys, and Zoot and Al Cohn and Sweets. Sweets was my idol. Harry Edison. You know from the Basie band. And it meant a lot to me. I once said, recently, Snooky Young came in. You know who he is?

And Snooky and I — he played for us when I managed the Hines Brothers. And I wrote their act and conducted. And I’m standing with Snooky and I said, “hey Snook,” I said, “you know I can’t believe I know you and you are my friend.” He said, “what are you saying?” He said, “you were my boss with the Hines Brothers.” Because I managed them. And I said, “no I was never your boss,” I said, “we worked together. But you are Snooky Young. And I saw you play in the Lunceford band and I know you.” He couldn’t understand that.
I know. Those guys, they don’t think of themselves like we do.

Yeah. Exactly. It’s always, and the thing with our band, I feel when those guys like, rest their soul, like Sweets and Clark Terry and Tommy Newsom and they come and said, “boy that band sounds good.” And that’s what makes me go even further in my belief, which is almost total. But they won’t tell you that because they’re your friend. Because they played with the greats. And they’re not going to tell you, and I know they’re not, but they go, “Stanley,” you know, “Sherrie.” See they’re secure. The ones that are not secure,
yeah they’re playing, women, all right. Because they’re threatened. See? When you’re not threatened, you’re secure. There’s got to be room for everybody. See?
